title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

report.summary: New FASD method decouples knowledge erasure from refusal behavior in multimodal LLMs, achieving genuine 'honest ignorance' rather than surface-level unlearning.
report.background: Machine unlearning has moved from a legal curiosity to a core requirement for deployed AI. Regulations such as GDPR's right to erasure, copyright disputes over training data, and safety teams needing to strip dangerous capabilities all demand that a model actually stop knowing something. Most multimodal LLM (MLLM) unlearning work, however, is judged by a shallow test: does the model still print the target information? That metric hides two problems. Knowledge-suppression methods like gradient ascent often push the model into confabulation, inventing plausible but false facts about the erased subject. Refusal training, meanwhile, only changes surface behavior: the model says 'I don't know' to an open prompt but still picks the correct answer on a multiple-choice probe, proving the knowledge remains intact. This paper argues evaluation and method design must separate what the model knows from what it says.
key_points: The paper identifies two hidden failure modes in current MLLM unlearning. Suppression-based methods cause confabulation, where the model hallucinates fake facts about the unlearned subject. Refusal-based methods only mask behavior: models decline open queries yet still score correctly under multiple-choice probing, revealing the underlying knowledge was never removed.

Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD) splits the problem into two channels. The behavior channel distills refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself, and critically masks target tokens from the teacher distribution so the forgotten concepts are not accidentally re-taught during distillation.

The knowledge channel suppresses ground-truth answer spans directly, independent of whatever text the model generates. This means erasure is enforced at the level of internal knowledge rather than the visible output, closing the gap that let earlier methods leak answers through indirect probing.

FASD targets 'honest ignorance' as its objective: a state where the model truly loses the target knowledge and simultaneously learns to acknowledge that absence, accurately recognizing the boundaries of its own knowledge instead of bluffing.
Experiments show FASD unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. Code and data are promised upon publication.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes unlearning from a compliance checkbox into a measurable property with two independent axes: what the model knows and what it admits. Safety and legal teams get a harder benchmark, since multiple-choice probing becomes the standard leakage test rather than open-ended refusal rates. Developers building fine-tuning or model-editing pipelines will likely adopt self-distillation plus token masking as a reusable recipe, and evaluation suites will need updating to catch confabulation. For regular users, the practical effect is more trustworthy models: instead of confidently inventing details about a person or topic it was supposed to forget, a model trained this way can say it does not know and mean it. That reduces both misinformation and false-privacy assurances.
report.tools: To follow up, watch Hugging Face transformers and PEFT for reproducing self-distillation experiments, MLLMU-Bench for standardized multimodal unlearning evaluation, and the OpenUnlearning suite for comparable metrics on knowledge retention versus erasure. Configure Accelerate or DeepSpeed for the dual-channel training loop, and track the authors' promised code release for the masking implementation. For probing-based leakage tests, build custom multiple-choice harnesses on top of lm-evaluation-harness.
